Frozen Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models can be improved at inference time without modifying weights, but existing approaches either apply correction unconditionally or require prohibitive compute.
We propose ACR-VLA, a lightweight adaptive correction pipeline for frozen flow-matching VLAs. At each control step, the pipeline draws $K{=}2$ action samples in a single batched forward pass and uses their pairwise $L_2$ distance ($\rho{=}0.9979$ vs.\ $K{=}10$ sample variance) as a per-step uncertainty gate. Low-uncertainty steps output the argmin-to-centroid sample directly; high-uncertainty steps apply bounded residual correction via a Correction Residual Module (CRM). The pipeline uses at most two VLA forward passes---performance gains come from learned correction, not additional sampling.
We validate ACR-VLA across three flow-matching VLAs (SmolVLA 0.4B, $\pi_{0.5}$ 3.6B, OpenVLA-OFT 7B) on four LIBERO benchmark suites. On SmolVLA, ACR-VLA achieves $18.3$\% on LIBERO-Object ($+$7.3\,pp vs.\ VLA-only) and $35.0$\% on LIBERO-Spatial ($+$5.6\,pp), matching fixed-$K{=}10$ unconditional correction with 80\% fewer forward passes. Systematic analysis reveals that learned correction is the active mechanism (55--78\% of the gain), while multi-sampling provides enabling centering---random selection alone fails to improve over VLA-only on either benchmark.

\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related_work}

\looseness=-1 \paragraph{VLA robustness.} Vision-language-action models have progressed from tokenized prediction~\cite{brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,ghosh2024octo} to generative approaches based on diffusion~\cite{chi2023diffusion_policy} and flow matching~\cite{black2024pi0,shukor2025smolvla}. Robustness evaluations~\cite{fei2025liberoplus} show that current VLAs lose over 65\,pp under deployment perturbations. Training-time defenses (SRPO~\cite{srpo2025}, RobustVLA~\cite{robustvla2025}, DiG-Flow~\cite{digflow2025}, TT-VLA~\cite{liu2026ttvla}) improve robustness but require retraining or reward engineering.

\looseness=-1 \paragraph{Inference-time correction.} Among frozen-VLA methods, ReconVLA~\cite{chen2026reconvla} provides uncertainty quantification but no learned correction; SC-VLA~\cite{liu2026scvla} requires task-level RL; VLA-Pilot~\cite{li2025vlapilot} uses evolutionary optimization at 2.41\,s per step. A2C2~\cite{a2c2_2025} is the closest concurrent work: it learns a correction head addressing \emph{temporal staleness} within action chunks. Our pipeline targets a complementary problem---\emph{initial action quality}---with multi-sample centering, explicit magnitude control, and adaptive per-step compute allocation. Residual policy learning~\cite{silver2018residual,johannink2019residual} shares the additive-correction structure; magnitude control is the central challenge, addressed by gating~\cite{jiang2024transic}, RL-bounded clipping~\cite{xiao2026pld}, or decay~\cite{pan2025drc}. Our CRM uses fixed $L_2$ norm clipping with supervised loss, requiring no RL or online rollouts.

\looseness=-1 \paragraph{Inference-time compute scaling.} Test-time scaling in LLMs~\cite{snell2024scaling} improves quality via best-of-N selection. RoVer~\cite{dai2025rover} transfers this to VLAs with a reward model; DA-SIP~\cite{chun2025dasip} adapts denoising steps per difficulty. Our analysis shows a different pattern in continuous action spaces: learned correction dominates over selection (Section~\ref{sec:main_results}), motivating a $K{=}2$ uncertainty probe that triggers correction rather than scaling sample count.
